On August 4, 2026, Bending Spoons agreed to acquire Airtable for US$1.285 billion in an all-cash deal, a staggering drop from the US$11.7 billion valuation Airtable commanded at the peak of the 2021 software boom.
The most valuable no-code company of the last decade just changed hands for a number that would have been unthinkable five years ago. On August 4, 2026, Bending Spoons agreed to acquire Airtable for US$1.285 billion in an all-cash deal, a staggering drop from the US$11.7 billion valuation Airtable commanded at the peak of the 2021 software boom.
Bending Spoons buys Airtable for $1.285B, far below its 2021 valuation. What the deal signals for SaaS in an AI-first world.
Airtable, founded in 2013, built its name on a simple but powerful idea: give teams a tool that feels as easy as a spreadsheet but works like a database. That combination turned it into the backbone for how hundreds of thousands of teams organize projects, track inventory, manage content calendars, and build lightweight internal apps without writing code. As of June 2026, the company was generating roughly US$480 million in annual recurring revenue, still growing more than 20% year over year, and counted more than 500,000 organizations as customers, including 80% of the Fortune 100.
Airtable co-founder and CEO Howie Liu noted that "more than 500,000 organizations rely on Airtable to power their most critical work." If the buyer's name is unfamiliar, the apps it owns are not. Bending Spoons is the Italian company that has quietly assembled a portfolio of well-known consumer and productivity brands: Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Harvest, StreamYard, komoot, Remini, and even AOL. As of March 2026, its products reached more than 500 million monthly active users and over 9 million paying customers.

Airtable is not a struggling company. Its annual recurring revenue was around $480 million as of June 2026, growing over 20% year over year.
After the 2022 acquisition, Bending Spoons let go most of the US team and moved operations to Europe. Then pricing moved. Customers who paid $37 a year for the Pro plan before 2023 were being charged $250 a year by 2026, according to The Pragmatic Engineer, which describes the strategy as maximizing revenue rather than the number of customers.

results.content:
Is Airtable still the right tool to build your workflows around after the Bending Spoons deal?  
I get why you might be asking. On August 4, 2026, Bending Spoons agreed to acquire Airtable in a [$1.285 billion deal](https://investors.bendingspoons.com/newsroom/bending-spoons-agrees-to-acquire-airtable), although the purchase has not closed yet.  
So I compared five Airtable alternatives worth considering: [Monday.com](https://try.monday.com/nawgrzid79nh), ClickUp, [Zoho Creator](https://go.zoho.com/luhn), Baserow, and Notion.  
That doesn’t mean Airtable is suddenly a bad choice. But when a tool holds your data, [automations](https://crmside.com/business-automation-statistics/), and day-to-day processes, a major ownership change is a good reason to check your options.  
Here’s which one makes the most sense for the way you work.
## **Why Are Airtable Users Looking for Alternatives After the Bending Spoons Deal?**  
When a tool becomes part of your daily workflow, an ownership change gets your attention.  
That’s especially true with Airtable. Teams don’t just use it for simple lists. They build [CRMs](https://crmside.com/crm-for-small-business/), content calendars, approval systems, project trackers, automations, and internal databases around it.  
So when Bending Spoons agreed to acquire Airtable in August 2026, some users naturally started asking what could change next.  
Could pricing shift? Could product priorities move in a different direction? Will smaller teams still get the same attention? What happens to integrations, automations, or features people rely on every day?  
Those are fair questions, but they’re still questions.  
Bending Spoons has said it plans to invest in Airtable for the long term, and the acquisition had not yet closed as of August 12, 2026. So there’s no good reason to assume Airtable is about to become worse overnight.  
Still, this is a smart time to look at your options.  
Think of it like having a spare key. You may never need it, but you’ll be glad you know where it is if something changes later.  
The goal isn’t to panic and migrate everything tomorrow. It’s to understand which Airtable alternatives could handle your most important workflows if pricing, limits, support, or product direction ever stop working for you.
# **FAQ**  
## **Who acquired Airtable?**  
Bending Spoons announced on **August 4, 2026** that it had entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Airtable for **$1.285 billion in enterprise value**. Including Airtable’s net cash, the deal implies an equity value of roughly $2.25 billion.  
The acquisition has not closed yet. Bending Spoons says it expects the transaction to close later in 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. Until then, Airtable and Bending Spoons continue to operate independently.
